objectives: Use λ = ax/D for two slits and nλ = d sin θ for a grating
Prove λ = ax/D using two similar triangles
Describe how to measure the wavelength of laser light

questions.a: Waves with a constant phase difference (so the same frequency).

questions.q: Two points on a wave of wavelength 4.0 mm are 1.4 mm apart. Find their phase difference in degrees.
State the path difference for a maximum and for a minimum in two-source interference.
Calculate the wavelength of light of frequency 5.0 × 10^14 Hz in a vacuum.
Define diffraction. When is it most noticeable?
questions.a: The spreading of a wave through a gap or round an obstacle. Most when the gap is about the same size as λ.

questions.q: Write 0.25 mm and 650 nm in metres, in standard form.

engage.hook: In 1801 most scientists agreed with Newton: light is a stream of particles. Thomas Young shone light through two slits.
engage.imageDescription: torch beam drawn as both a wave and a stream of particles

reveal.question: If light were particles, what would the screen show? What did Young see?
reveal.answer: Particles would give two bright strips. Young saw lots of evenly spaced bright and dark fringes. Only waves interfere like that.

learn.heading: Young's double-slit experiment

items: A laser lights two narrow slits, a fraction of a millimetre apart.
Laser light is monochromatic and coherent.
The screen is several metres away.
Light diffracts at each slit. The two beams overlap and interfere.
Evenly spaced bright and dark fringes.
Bright: path difference nλ. Dark: path difference (n + ½)λ.

learn.imageDescription: light through a double slit making bright and dark interference fringes on a screen

learn.heading: The double-slit equation

components.name: fringe separation, bright to next bright

learn.example: Only works when a is much smaller than D. a = 0.50 mm, x = 2.4 mm, D = 2.0 m: λ = (5.0 × 10^-4 × 2.4 × 10^-3) ÷ 2.0 = 6.0 × 10^-7 m
learn.imageDescription: lamp, single slit, double slit and screen seen from above, with fringes on the screen

learn.heading: The diffraction grating equation

components.name: angle from the central (zero order) maximum

learn.imageDescription: laser beam through a diffraction grating, central and second order maxima on a screen

items: Hundreds of slits per mm, so d is tiny.
Maxima are much brighter and sharper than with two slits.
Angles are large, so they are easy to measure.
No small-angle approximation: use sin θ exactly.
sin θ cannot be more than 1, so n ≤ d/λ. Round down.

learn.heading: Proof step 1: path difference = a sin θ

boxes.header: The small triangle at the slits
items: Rays to a far point P leave both slits almost parallel, at θ to the centre line.
Draw S_1N at right angles to the rays. The angle at S_1 is also θ.
Light from S_2 travels the extra distance S_2N.
S_2N = a sin θ

learn.imageDescription: close-up of two slits with the small right-angled triangle and path difference a sin theta

learn.heading: Proof step 2: tan θ = x/D

boxes.header: The big triangle to the screen
items: From the middle of the slits to P, the first bright fringe.
P is a distance x from the centre O. The screen is D away.
tan θ = {x/D}
Both triangles are right-angled and both contain θ.
So the same θ links the slits to the screen.

learn.imageDescription: double slit to screen with the big right-angled triangle, D along the bottom and x up the screen

learn.heading: Proof step 3: the small-angle approximation

items: D is a few metres. x is a few millimetres.
So θ is a small fraction of a degree.
For small θ in radians: sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ
So sin θ ≈ {x/D}

learn.imageDescription: thin right-angled triangle with a small angle and a table of sin, tan and theta in radians

learn.heading: Proof step 4: λ = ax/D

items: Constructive when a sin θ = nλ.
First bright fringe, n = 1: a sin θ = λ
a × {x/D} = λ, so λ = {ax/D}
The nth bright fringe is nx from the centre, so every gap is x.

learn.imageDescription: double slit fringes with path differences 0, lambda and 2 lambda and both triangles highlighted

build.q: OCR: double slit, D = 3.5 m, a = 1.5 mm. Central fringe to 6th order fringe = 9 mm. What is the wavelength?
The proof replaces sin θ with tan θ. Why is that allowed?
build.explanation: θ is tiny because x is millimetres and D is metres, so sin θ ≈ tan θ.

build.q: The screen is moved from 1.5 m to 3.0 m from the slits. What happens to the fringe separation x?
build.explanation: x = λD/a, so x is proportional to D.

build.q: OCR: 600 nm light, grating, screen 3.0 m away. The two 1st order maxima are 1.42 m apart. What is the line spacing in m?
What is the path difference at the first order bright fringe?
build.explanation: Bright fringes: path difference nλ, and n = 1 here.

build.q: OCR: 640 nm laser light, grating line spacing 3.3 × 10^-6 m. What is the total number of bright spots seen?
build.explanation: n ≤ d/λ = 5.2, so n = 5 each side. 5 + 5 + the central spot = 11.

questions.q: 10 fringe gaps measure 8.3 mm. a = 1.6 mm, D = 2.5 m. Calculate λ.
Same slits and screen (a = 1.6 mm, D = 2.5 m) with 470 nm light. Find x.
Blue laser, 455 nm. a = 0.90 mm, D = 3.0 m. How far is the 1st bright fringe from the centre?

worked.prompt: A grating has 300 lines per mm. A green laser (532 nm) shines on it normally. Find the angle of the 2nd order maximum.

yourTurn.prompt: A grating has 600 lines per mm. The 1st order maximum is at 22.3°. Find the wavelength.
yourTurn.answer: d = 1.67 μm, so λ = d sin 22.3° = 633 nm

wrongWorking: a = 0.40 mm, D = 2.5 m. 8 fringe gaps measure 30 mm.
build.errorType: used the width of several fringes as x

statements.text: Moving the screen further away spreads the fringes out.
Slits further apart give wider fringes.
statements.correction: x = λD/a, so a bigger a gives fringes closer together.

statements.text: Blue light gives wider fringes than red light.
statements.correction: Blue has a shorter λ, so its fringes are closer together.

statements.text: λ = ax/D works for a diffraction grating.
statements.correction: Grating angles are large. Use nλ = d sin θ with no small-angle approximation.

statements.text: The central fringe is bright because the path difference there is zero.

build.title: Practical 1: wavelength of laser light with a double slit
build.heading: Practical 1: wavelength of laser light with a double slit
steps: Darken the room. Shine the laser through the double slit onto a screen 2 to 5 m away.
Measure D, slits to screen, with a tape measure. Make D as big as the room allows.
Measure across 10 or more fringe gaps. Divide by the number of gaps to get x.
Measure a with a travelling microscope or vernier calipers, or use the value given.
Repeat for several values of D. Plot x against D: the gradient is λ/a.
Work out % uncertainties (a is usually the biggest). Then λ = ax/D.
build.warning: Class 2 laser. Never look into the beam or point it at anyone. Use a matt screen, no shiny surfaces.
build.imageDescription: laser shining through a double slit onto a screen showing a row of bright spots

questions.q: Why measure across 10 fringe gaps and divide, instead of measuring one gap?
questions.a: The uncertainty is spread over 10 gaps, so the % uncertainty in x is 10 times smaller.

questions.q: Why is the screen put several metres away?
questions.a: Bigger D gives bigger x, so the % uncertainties in x and D are smaller.

questions.q: a = 0.50 ± 0.05 mm. What is the % uncertainty in a?

build.title: Practical 2: wavelength with a diffraction grating
build.heading: Practical 2: wavelength with a diffraction grating
steps: Laser through a grating of known lines per mm, onto a screen over 1 m away.
Measure D, grating to screen, with a tape measure.
Measure between the two 1st order spots. Halve it to get y.
θ = tan^-1(y/D). Find d = 1 ÷ lines per metre.
λ = d sin θ ÷ n. Repeat for n = 2 and compare.
Better: plot d sin θ against n. The gradient is λ.
build.warning: Class 2 laser. Never look into the beam or point it at anyone. Use a matt screen, no shiny surfaces.
build.imageDescription: laser through a diffraction grating, central and second order maxima on a screen

questions.q: Why measure between the two 1st order spots and halve it?
questions.a: The centre of the central spot is hard to find. A bigger distance also has a smaller % uncertainty.

questions.q: Why is there no small-angle approximation here?
questions.a: Grating angles are large (often 10° to 40°), so sin θ and tan θ are not equal.

questions.q: A grating has 300 lines per mm. Find d.

developing.q: Explain why the central fringe in a Young double-slit experiment is bright.
developing.a: Both slits are the same distance from the centre. Path difference 0, waves arrive in phase: constructive interference.

developing.q: A red laser (635 nm) lights slits 0.90 mm apart. The screen is 3.0 m away. Find the fringe separation.
The screen is moved further from the slits. What happens to the fringe separation? Use λ = ax/D.
developing.a: It increases. x = λD/a, so x is proportional to D.

reaching.q: A grating has 500 lines per mm. Light of 450 nm hits it normally. Find the angle of the 2nd order maximum.
Transmitters 0.20 m apart emit 10 GHz microwaves in phase. D = 4.0 m. Find the distance between a maximum and the next minimum.
590 nm light gives fringes 1.2 mm apart on a screen 1.5 m from the slits. Find the slit separation a.

mastering.q: Show that x ≈ λD/a for a double slit. Draw both triangles and state the approximations you make.
mastering.a: Path difference = a sin θ = λ for the 1st bright fringe. tan θ = x/D. a ≪ D so rays parallel; small θ so sin θ ≈ tan θ. So λ = ax/D.

mastering.q: OCR: a grating with 800 lines per mm is used with the 486 nm hydrogen-beta line. Calculate the angle of the 2nd order line.
The laser is swapped for a white light source. Describe and explain the pattern on the screen.
mastering.a: White central fringe: path difference 0 for every colour. Side fringes coloured, blue inside, red outside, as x ∝ λ. Further out the colours overlap.

groups.stem: In an experiment to measure the wavelength of yellow light from a sodium lamp, a beam of light from a lamp passes through a pair of narrow slits S_1 and S_2. This produces a pattern of regularly spaced bright and dark lines, called fringes, on a screen as shown in Fig. 5.1. A student makes the following measurements: distance S_1S_2 = 0.8 mm, distance AB on screen = 6.0 mm, distance from slits to screen = 1.6 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength, in nanometre, of the sodium light.

parts.label: c
parts.text: To reduce the uncertainty in the calculated value of the wavelength, one student suggests making a different slide with a greater slit separation. Discuss whether you think this change will reduce the uncertainty.
parts.ms: Percentage uncertainty in a decreases (B1). Fringes move closer together / percentage uncertainty in x increases / actually measuring 5x so smaller effect / AW (B1). With both measurements to 0.1 mm, measurement of a gives larger improvement so decrease in uncertainty in λ (B1).
